context_blurb:
A brown haze over a city, a muddy river after a storm, a field stripped bare by the wind: each shows air, water or soil being dirtied or lost. Scientists measure where the harm comes from and test what stops it, from treatment plants and rows of trees to the light bulb in a lamp.

Pollution is anything harmful added to the air, the water or the soil. Burning fuels such as coal, gasoline and wood, in engines, power plants, factories and stoves, makes about 85 percent of the dirty air that people breathe. Farms, mines, dumps and everything else add a much smaller share.

Smoke is a mix of gases and solid specks. The finest specks of soot and ash are the worst danger to health: about 30 times thinner than a hair, they slip past the nose and throat deep into the lungs, and some reach the blood. Bigger flakes rarely get that far. Carbon monoxide, a poison gas, is a danger near the flames, but very little of it is found a short way off.

Rain and melting snow wash drips of oil from leaking cars, roads and parking lots into rivers, which carry it to the sea. In 2022 the National Academies, a group of leading American scientists, ranked this runoff from the land first among the sources of oil in North America's seas. Seeps from the seabed came second, and oil spills, the source most people picture, only third.

A drinking-water plant cleans river water in steps. First a chemical called alum makes dirt stick together in heavy clumps that sink, and filters of sand and gravel catch much of the rest. Near the end, a small dose of chlorine kills any germs the filters missed. Germs are living things too small to see, and some cause disease, so water can look clear and still be unsafe. A little chlorine stays in the water to keep killing germs in the pipes.

Untreated sewage, the dirty water from toilets and drains, spreads diseases such as cholera, and as it rots in a river it uses up the oxygen that fish need. At a sewage plant, heavy solids first sink in tanks of still water. Then bacteria feed on the waste and break it down, and like people these bacteria need oxygen, so pumps keep bubbling air through the tanks. Bacteria are not all harmful: the plant keeps these alive.

Soil carried off by water or wind is lost to erosion. Raindrops hit bare soil hard enough to splash specks loose, and the specks clog the surface into a crust, so less rain soaks in and more runs off, carrying soil away. Straw and stalks left on a field after the harvest take the blow of each falling raindrop, so the surface stays open and more rain soaks in. The straw is a shield, not a weight.

On steep hillsides, farmers build terraces, turning one long slope into a row of short, flat steps propped up by low walls. Rain landing on a flat step slows down and has time to soak in, and any soil it carries settles on the step instead of rushing downhill. On average, terraces cut soil loss about eleven times.

On flat plains, a row of trees along a field's edge, called a windbreak, slows the wind by half or more just behind it, and slower wind cannot lift and carry off dry soil. Its roots reach only a narrow strip near the row, so they are not what saves the field. After the dust storms of the 1930s, about 220 million trees were planted in such rows across the American plains.

Efficiency is how much of a machine's energy goes into its real job. An old incandescent bulb makes light by heating a thin wire until it glows, so more than 90 percent of its energy leaves as heat and only about a tenth or less becomes light. An LED, a light-emitting diode, wastes far less as heat: a 9-watt LED gives about as much light as a 60-watt old bulb. Energy is never used up; it only changes form, here from electricity into light and heat.
